title: Concerning the Going Concern

canonicalEdition.name: First edition
canonicalEdition.sourceProvenance: Frozen web bundle only: bibliographic records, table-of-contents evidence, official publication metadata, and narrow secondary summary support. Paraphrase-first; no full text frozen.

anchorSummary: This chapter focuses on the operating design of a real company at scale, where politics, executive selection, performance systems, and culture have to be managed intentionally instead of by founder instinct alone.
coreClaim: A growing company survives only if its leaders intentionally design the organization instead of assuming early-stage habits will scale on their own.
distinctMechanism: Horowitz treats the going concern as an organizational-design challenge: minimize politics, formalize the right systems, and match executives to the company's actual stage and needs.
requiredAnchors: Politics and process: growth makes informal signals and incentives more dangerous.
Executive fit is contextual: there is no universally great executive independent of company stage and need.
Culture and operating cadence must be programmed deliberately as the company scales.
specificApplications: Identify where informal startup habits are now creating political drift.
Evaluate executives for fit against stage, not prestige alone.
Use process to reduce ambiguity where growth has outpaced direct oversight.
commonMisreadings: Treating the chapter as a call for bureaucracy rather than for intentional design.
Assuming culture programs itself if the founder's values are merely sincere.
hardEdgeRequirement: Hard mode must show why refusing to formalize the right systems is not preserving startup agility but exporting confusion into a larger company.
thresholdQuestion: Which small-company habit becomes dangerous once the company is too large for informal coordination alone?
